articles.title: Trump’s Texas two-step: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, we dig into yet another visit to Texas from the president. Plus, Andrea Mitchell examines what has — and hasn’t — happened since Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel. — Adam Wollner Trump’s Texas two-step By Adam Wollner President Donald Trump is making his second trip in the past week to Texas tonight, highlighting how the midterm fight has shifted traditionally red terrain in the final stretch. He’s set to rally in San Antonio for state Attorney General Ken Paxton and congressional candidate Carlos De La Cruz. Paxton remains locked in a tight and expensive battle with Democrat James Talarico. And De La Cruz’s race in the 35th District, which was redrawn in the redistricting process last year to be more favorable to Republicans, has been more competitive than expected. While Trump would have carried the district under its new lines by 10 points in 2024, the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates the race as “lean Republican.” Notably absent from tonight’s rally? Gov. Greg Abbott, who cited a scheduling conflict.“Well, first, whenever he does show up, it leads to excitement among the base, and he does a good job of getting the base organized and turning out,” Abbott said yesterday of Trump. “Because of the schedule that I run, where I go to multiple cities a day doing events like this, already have events like this scheduled that day, and I will not be able to make it,” he added. Abbott is also facing a tougher re-election battle than Republicans anticipated at the outset of the cycle: He won his last three races for governor by double digits. But the broader political environment has proven treacherous for Republican candidates across the board. And now, national Democrats are under growing pressure to spend more resources on behalf of gubernatorial nominee Gina Hinojosa, who is at a major financial disadvantage against Abbott. Natasha Korecki reports that Latino leaders in Texas, including members of Congress, met with the Democratic Governors Association this morning to discuss Hinojosa’s campaign. In a letter, a group of Latino stakeholders in the state called on the DGA to “make a real meaningful investment of $3 million” into the race before early voting begins in less than two weeks. The DGA recently committed $1 million to the race, while Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker announced he would send $1 million to her campaign after already giving $200,000. (The New York Times first reported on those contributions.) Meanwhile, Abbott isn’t the only Republican on the ballot this fall who appears to be seeking some distance from Trump. Michigan GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers said in a new ad today that “we need to end this tariff war now.” The party’s candidate for governor in the state, John James, also put daylight between himself and Trump on tariffs and the Iran war at a debate last night. 🥊 More from the debate stage: In the Maine Senate race, Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson traded attacks over Trump, the cost of living and abortion. In Georgia’s race for governor, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson also sparred over Trump and the economy. And in the Iowa gubernatorial contest, Republican Zach Lahn’s residency history was a major topic. The Oct. 7 attack, three years later Analysis by Andrea Mitchell At dawn on a holiday weekend three years ago today, Israel was stunned when hordes of Hamas terrorists stormed across its border, slashing and and kidnapping revelers at an all-night music festival and rampaging through nearby settlements, or kibbutzim. In total, 1,200 Israelis and foreign nationals, including 46 U.S. citizens, were killed, while 251 were taken hostage. Thus began a war that shattered Israel’s confidence in its military superiority and ultimately transformed the region, sowing the seeds for the current war against Iran. Despite a ceasefire and hostage release, the conflict in the Gaza Strip and now the occupied West Bank continues at a slow burn with periodic outbreaks to this day. How could Israel have been so taken by surprise? Although Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has blocked an official investigation into how his country’s vaunted military could have been so blindsided, NBC News has confirmed authoritative reports on the colossal intelligence failure, including a stunning account that an all-woman border patrol’s early warnings were dismissed by male superiors. Inexplicably, it took more than six hours after the massacre for the country to mobilize a response. The human cost is incalculable. By the numbers, the Hamas-led Gaza Health Ministry estimates that about 75,000 people, including more than 44,000 children, have died in Gaza. Thousands more have been injured. Israel says it has lost 970 soldiers. Gaza has largely been leveled, its housing, schools and hospitals destroyed. The International Criminal Court, a United Nations entity that is not recognized by either Israel or the Trump administration, has cited both sides over allegations of war crimes. And the conflict has fueled cries of genocide against Israel by protesters in Europe and the U.S., an accusation that’s offensive to those in a country born as a refuge for survivors of the Holocaust. Based on a Biden administration plan, Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner finalized a ceasefire and release of surviving hostages, as well as the return of hostage remains. The White House promises that its Board of Peace — a group of world leaders each pledging $1 billion to a nongovernment entity led by President Donald Trump — is supposed to be recruiting a multinational peace-keeping force to disarm Hamas and get Israel to withdraw to a border buffer zone. Trump has said the Gaza Strip could be rebuilt as “The Riviera of the Middle East.” None of that has taken place. Now, Netanyahu faces a closely fought election in three weeks that has become a referendum on his conduct of the war in Gaza and failure to prevent it. His national security ministers are spearheading a campaign to seize as many Palestinian villages in the disputed West Bank as possible now as a hedge against a victory by a government less opposed to a Palestinian state. And Israel’s conduct of the war has become a political issue in the U.S. that could affect some of this year’s key midterm races as well as the Democratic Party’s nominating contest in 2028. Fiona Glisson contributed research. That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.title: 'I'm not bragging': Trump makes last-minute play for Nobel Peace Prize
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said he should win the Nobel Peace Prize for settling eight conflicts and keeping Iran from developing a nuclear weapon.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump is making a last-minute play for the Nobel Peace Prize, arguing that he should win the award that will be given out this week by a Norwegian organization for settling eight conflicts and intervening to keep Iran from developing a nuclear weapon .

Asked in the Oval Office about the prestigious prize that the Norwegian Nobel Institute will give out on Oct. 9, Trump alluded to the unsolved war between Russia and Ukraine that his administration has been trying to stop and said he should win the award for getting Israeli hostages back from Hamas.

"I'm not bragging. I'm just telling you the facts. No president probably has settled any wars. I settled eight wars, and big ones," Trump told journalists.

Trump has long groused about not winning the Nobel Peace Prize and campaigned heavily last year to be a recipient.

He did not win, in spite of his push, and has launched two military conflicts since. One in Venezuela – which the United States invaded in January, then arrested the country's leader on drug charges – and another in Iran – which America has been at war with since February, partly over the regime's desire to pursue a nuclear program.

Trump renewed his complaints on Oct. 7 that former President Barack Obama received the prize his first year in office. He also said he'd saved millions of lives and "stopped maybe the total obliteration of the world" through his bid to keep Iran from developing a nuclear weapon.

"I don't know what their decision's going to be. They have a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me. But whether I get it or not, I have done far more, and I think it would be a great discredit to them," Trump said.

Last year's Nobel Peace Prize winner, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, gifted Trump her award during an Oval Office visit, after the U.S. operation in Caracas that allowed Delcy Rodriguez to claim power.

"And since then, we've done a lot," Trump said.

articles.title: Nicolás Maduro and his wife expected to face new charges related to alleged torture of Americans
articles.summary: Former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and wife Cilia Flores face new charges tied to alleged torture of Americans in Manhattan court Thursday.
articles.body: Deposed Venezuelan Nicolás Maduro and his wife could face new charges tied to the alleged torture of Americans as prosecutors fight their efforts to have their criminal case thrown out. The additional charges are expected to be announced in Manhattan federal court, according to Fox News’ David Spunt and Jake Paronich. U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald is expected to speak after a 10:30 a.m. hearing. That hearing was scheduled to address a request by Maduro’s wife, Cilia Flores de Maduro, to be released from custody because of ongoing medical problems, including a heart condition. MADURO ALLY DEPORTED TO US OVER ALLEGED BILLION-DOLLAR CORRUPTION SCHEME TIED TO OIL, FOOD PROGRAM The expected charges would add to a case already involving allegations of cocaine trafficking, narco-terrorism and weapons offenses. Maduro and Flores deny the allegations and have sought to dismiss the case on sovereign immunity grounds. Federal prosecutors pushed back in a recent court filing, arguing neither defendant is entitled to that protection and that Venezuela has not asserted immunity on their behalf. The government noted that the U.S. has not recognized Maduro as Venezuela’s head of state since January 2019. "The defendants are former rogue officials of a formerly rogue state with no entitlement to immunity," prosecutors wrote. THE UNLIKELY SOUTH AMERICAN ALLY HELPING LEAD TRUMP'S DRUG CARTEL CRACKDOWN They argued that foreign sovereign immunity is "a matter of grace and comity on the part of the U.S., and not a restriction imposed by the Constitution." Prosecutors also argued that the alleged cocaine trafficking, narco-terrorism and weapons offenses violated the law rather than served any legitimate government function. Maduro’s attorneys argued in their motion that the court lacks jurisdiction because he is recognized as Venezuela’s head of state. Flores separately filed a motion seeking dismissal on sovereign immunity grounds. Maduro is also challenging the narco-terrorism conspiracy count. His lawyers said he vehemently denies involvement in drug trafficking intended to benefit groups allegedly engaged in terrorism and argued that prosecutors have not met the elements required for the charge. VENEZUELAN GANG MEMBERS WHO ENTERED US ILLEGALLY PLEAD GUILTY TO GUNNING DOWN TWO UNARMED AMERICANS The government countered that the "prohibited drug activity had a nexus to and intended effect on the United States." Prosecutors allege Maduro and other defendants participated in cocaine trafficking that resulted in thousands of tons of cocaine being distributed to the United States, funding and supporting violent terrorist organizations. Meanwhile, Flores’ attorneys have proposed home confinement with GPS monitoring, round-the-clock armed surveillance, surrender of her travel documents and a court-approved third-party custodian. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Her lawyer said she was recovering from a complete hysterectomy before her arrest and receiving monthly injections for mitral valve prolapse. She may now need cardiac catheterization, which could lead to more invasive heart procedures, according to her release motion. "Her medical condition is significant and her current housing, despite best efforts, is inadequate to allow for proper recovery from cardiac surgery," her attorney wrote Flores’ defense also argues she poses no danger to the community and denies the allegations against her.

articles.title: 100-shot Somali gang gun battle rocks Minnesota as sheriff warns 'we're in trouble'
articles.summary: CCTV captured a gunfight that left 97 casings in Bloomington as Somali gang violence across Minnesota's Twin Cities draws national attention.
articles.body: Violence tied to Somali-American gangs in the Twin Cities metro erupted in recent days, with law enforcement recovering nearly 100 casings after a gunfight captured on a resident’s surveillance camera — as officials warn they need help to contain the problem before it escalates. The warning follows a burst of violence across several Twin Cities suburbs — including a Bloomington shootout that left nearly 100 shell casings and another shooting in Eden Prairie — as law enforcement says the incidents have entered a retaliation cycle and officials race to disrupt the groups before the violence evolves into more entrenched drug- and money-driven crime. "We have the opportunity to fix it," Ramsey County Sheriff Bob Fletcher said of a surge in Somali gang violence across the Twin Cities — but warned authorities could be facing a much more difficult problem if the groups escalate the resources they use. 3 DEAD, INCLUDING SUSPECTED GUNMAN, AND 3 OFFICERS INJURED IN MINNEAPOLIS SHOOTING "It’s early. Once they evolve into drugs, we’re in trouble. Once they evolve into money, more money, we are in trouble," said Fletcher, whose county is anchored by St. Paul and runs along the west bank of the Mississippi River. Fletcher estimated that about 300 juveniles are involved and said part of the problem lies in the Somali gangs’ relative novelty to local law enforcement and what he characterized as a reluctance to aggressively prosecute offenders across the river in Minneapolis. TRUMP’S LAW-AND-ORDER BLITZ MARKS ONE YEAR WITH EYE-POPPING HAUL OF SUSPECTS, GUNS IN BLUE CITY "We need more people focused on this problem. Because 50 kids in this 300 need to go to jail, 25 need to be prosecuted by the feds for RICO and and another 25 need to be prosecuted at the local level. Take 50 of the most active out of the mix, and we will see dramatic changes," he said. He ascribed some of the reticence to neighboring Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, saying she has not been sufficiently "aggressive" in prosecuting such offenders. FEDERAL JUDGE REFERS PHILADELPHIA DA LARRY KRASNER TO DOJ FOR POSSIBLE CRIMINAL INVESTIGATION "One of the misconceptions is that somehow when you prosecute people, put them in jail that you're destituting them to some terrible life. This is how kids get corrected," he said. Moriarty’s office pushed back on the assertion, with spokesman Daniel Borgertpoepping saying the neighboring communities are "looking for solutions" and that Moriarty’s prosecutors "communicate daily with law enforcement [and] will participate in any group that moves us toward sustainable public safety." "The way we approach prosecution of violent crime is consistent regardless of the race or ethnicity of those involved," Borgertpoepping said. Meanwhile, residents across the metro region expressed outrage to local officials over the violence and what they described as a growing threat to public safety. Jared Scribner, a resident of nearby Edina, criticized officials for calling the issue "gun violence" and demanded they "confront what is happening even when the facts are politically uncomfortable." Scribner said violence associated with the gangs erupted at a local homecoming event and at a park. MEMPHIS MOM SAYS TRUMP BROUGHT PEACE TO STREETS AS DEMOCRATIC DA BATTLES TASK FORCE OVERSIGHT "We don't need more virtue signaling, yard signs, DEI initiatives, or community conversations that lead to nowhere. We need competent government, accountability, and safe neighborhoods," he said, also blaming Moriarty’s office for "refu[sing]" to properly address the issue. He also suggested officials have sometimes generalized the ethnicity of those involved, remarking that it "feels more comfortable for some people to say East African. I don't even know that that's a fair term, because 98% of these gang members are Somalians." In nearby Bloomington, where about 100 casings were recovered from the scene of a late-night firefight that appeared to involve automatic weapons, Police Chief Booker Hodges took a confrontational tack toward the suspects who remained at large — while warning they do not fit the typical stereotype of gang members. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "They're coming from two parent homes, living in apartment buildings with $3,500 a month rent, driving Beamers and Mercedes. They're not dealing with money. There's no drugs in the house. They're purchasing legal firearms," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "To those of you who did this shooting, you know that I know that you know that I that we know who you are. So my suggestion is: you turn yourself in. Let's stop playing these games with you running around out here doing all this stuff," Hodges warned — as the violence draws national attention.

articles.title: DNC sues administration over taxpayer-funded pro-Trump TV ads
articles.summary: Trump announced this week that he and his PAC, MAGA Inc., would pay for the ads moving forward following bipartisan criticism.
articles.body: The Democratic National Committee sued the Trump administration Wednesday over its taxpayer-funded advertisements that portray President Donald Trump in a favorable light, alleging the ads violate federal laws on government spending and propaganda. The DNC cited a measure Trump signed into law this year that says funds appropriated by Congress can’t be used “for publicity or propaganda purposes within the United States not heretofore authorized by Congress.” The lawsuit also cites the Anti-Deficiency Act, which bars spending government money that hasn’t been appropriated by Congress, and the Purpose Statute, which says taxpayer funds can be used only for the specific purposes approved by Congress. The DNC said the administration’s use of taxpayer dollars for “campaign-style advertisements” deprived Democrats “of a fair electoral process by adding public funds to the resources available to support Republican candidates.” The use of public funds places Democratic candidates at an electoral disadvantage, it argued. The ads, launched last month, sparked criticism from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, many of whom questioned their legality. Trump reversed course Monday, announcing on Truth Social he would no longer use government funds for the ads and saying he and his PAC, MAGA Inc., would foot the bill moving forward, instead. He didn’t say whether the government would be reimbursed for the ads that already ran. Reached for comment on the DNC lawsuit, the White House pointed NBC News to Trump’s Truth Social post. The Department of Homeland Security and the Office of Management and Budget, which are named as defendants in addition to Trump and the White House, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment on the lawsuit. Since Trump’s announcement, several of the ads have continued to run with the disclaimer that they were paid for by the U.S. government. Asked by NBC News whether those were paid for before or after Trump pledged to cover the costs, the White House wouldn’t say either way. A person familiar with the ads said that the ad buy for the spots, placed before Trump’s Monday announcement, will end this week. Afterwards, the person said, outside groups will begin paying for the ads. NBC News has reported that a $20 million contract was awarded to a Maryland firm for the ad campaign. AdImpact, a political ad-tracking firm, estimated that at least $10 million had been spent to air the ads through Monday. Attorneys for the DNC asked a federal judge in Washington to find that the administration acted unlawfully “by developing and airing the propaganda ads using Congressionally appropriated funds” and to prevent it from using those funds to develop and air the ads in the future. DNC Chair Ken Martin condemned the administration for using taxpayer dollars as Americans struggle with a rising cost of living. “Americans deserve better than to have their hard-earned tax dollars used for Trump’s illegal schemes,” he said in a statement Wednesday. The federal money for the ads came from funds intended for Customs and Border Protection, an arm of DHS. NBC News reported that CBP leadership was cut out of the decision to run the ads. Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr, a Trump appointee, said last week that the ads didn’t merit FCC review, arguing that they weren’t “anything at all out of the ordinary.” The White House has defended the ads by calling them “clearly not political” and claiming they were about “reminding Americans to love their country.” It has also pointed to other administrations’ use of public safety announcements.

articles.title: How Americans rank Trump among US presidents
articles.summary: After ranking himself the "greatest U.S. president," Trump got a decidedly different verdict from Americans in new poll.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump declared himself "The Greatest" U.S. president last month, placing himself above Abraham Lincoln, George Washington and Franklin D. Roosevelt in his personal ranking of American presidents .

A new YouGov poll suggests most Americans aren't on the same page. Nearly half of respondents rated Trump a presidential "failure," making him the most negatively rated current or former president included in the survey.

Presidents Lincoln, Washington and John F. Kennedy ranked among the poll's most admired presidents, while Trump and Presidents Joe Biden and Richard Nixon received the most negative assessments.

YouGov's findings diverged significantly from the rankings Trump shared in September.

Rather than viewing Trump as one of the nation's greatest presidents, 48% of respondents rated him a "failure," the highest share of any president measured in the survey. Biden was next at 35%, followed by Nixon at 28%.

YouGov grouped Trump, Biden and Nixon among the country's most negatively rated presidents.

Trump's own ranking placed Lincoln, Washington and Roosevelt in the tier below his self-designated spot as "The Greatest." In the YouGov survey, however, Lincoln topped the list of "consensus greats," with 57% rating him as great. Washington followed at 52%, while Kennedy ranked third at 37%.

articles.title: Anti-Israel groups rally across US on October 7 anniversary, chanting 'long live the intifada'
articles.summary: Anti-Israel groups chanted "long live the intifada" and celebrated the Hamas attack as October 7 anniversary protests swept across the country.
articles.body: On the third anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel, nonprofits and a number of anti-Israel organizations mobilized and rallied for demonstrations across the country, with some waving Palestinian flags, chanting "long live the intifada" and lauding the Hamas-planned ambush that killed more than a thousand civilians. A number of demonstrations took place in New York, California and other states – with nonprofits in the Singham network organizing and staging larger rallies set for this weekend, intentionally scheduled on and around the anniversary of the Hamas terrorist attack. At 12:30 p.m., organizers from the NYU Students for Justice in Palestine staged a walkout in Washington Square Park as part of their "NYU WEEK OF RAGE," where they said in a social media post they remain "steadfast in our commitment to Palestinian liberation." DUKE REINSTATES STUDENTS FOR JUSTICE IN PALESTINE AFTER SUSPENSION OVER ANTISEMITISM CONCERNS Separately, anti-Israel demonstrators arrived at the gates of Columbia University at 2 p.m., where encampments and riots embattled the campus for years after Oct. 7, 2023. As students filtered in and out of the gates, now guarded by heavy security, demonstrators from The Columbia Intifada and others chanted "globalize the intifada" through a megaphone. Columbia University has previously told Fox News Digital that the Columbia Intifada is not officially associated with the Ivy League school. At 4 p.m., some of the same groups who were protesting at Columbia traveled to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s office at City Hall, with Palestinian flags flying and chants echoing throughout the Financial District of Manhattan. FORMER HAMAS HOSTAGE COUNTERS HASAN PIKER’S UT AUSTIN EVENT WITH HER STORY OF SURVIVAL Mamdani weighed in on the anniversary earlier on Wednesday morning, saying "we grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors" who are dealing with the loss experienced on Oct. 7, 2023, before blasting Israel for an "ongoing genocide in Gaza." "The suffering did not begin nor end that day," Mamdani posted to X. "It instead continued through the Israeli government’s devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza, in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians — including more than 21,000 children." On Mamdani’s schedule for the anniversary of Oct. 7, he is set to meet with "Palestinian New Yorkers" following a vigil for the Israeli victims of the Hamas attack. MAMDANI ROASTED FOR STAYING TIGHT-LIPPED ON 'WAR CRIMINAL' PEZESHKIAN AFTER RAGING ABOUT NETANYAHU In California, Students for Justice in Palestine UCLA mobilized at Bruin Plaza on the Los Angeles campus, echoing similar messages to separate groups across the country. Agitators at UC Davis celebrated the terrorist attack, calling for "glory to the resistance" and referring to Oct. 7 as the "anniversary of the al-Aqsa Flood." Operation Al-Aqsa Flood is the military code name given by Hamas for the attack three years ago. UC BERKELEY SLAMMED AFTER ANTI-ISRAEL GROUP HOSTS FAILED SUICIDE BOMBER AS GUEST EVENT SPEAKER: 'CESSPOOL' On Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led terrorists stormed into southern Israel from the Gaza Strip, converging on a music festival in a surprise ambush that killed roughly 1,200 people. The attackers abducted more than 250 people and took them into Gaza as hostages, triggering a conflict that remains ongoing. The coordinated, organized events held Wednesday shed light on the protest infrastructure that has fueled many of the anti-Israel protests since October 2023, with Singham-backed groups like the People’s Forum and CodePink consistently in attendance. On Tuesday, the People’s Forum collaborated with Shut it Down 4 Palestine to prepare for a separate protest that will take place on Saturday in Washington Square Park "to stand against three years of continued genocide in Gaza," according to their social media post. INTEL EXPERT SAYS SINGHAM NETWORK IS MORE THAN A NONPROFIT SCANDAL—IT'S A SECURITY THREAT A Fox News Digital investigation revealed Singham has donated $22.44 million to the People's Forum Inc. Last month, CodePink, which was founded by Singham’s wife, Jodie Evans, marched alongside communist and Marxist groups in protest of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s speaking at the United Nations General Assembly. Singham, a 72-year-old American who sold his tech company for $785 million in 2017 and now lives in Shanghai, has funneled $278 million into the broad network of nonprofits since 2017, according to a Fox News Digital investigation. These groups regularly organize and participate in anti-ICE, anti-Israel and pro-Iran demonstrations. The Southern District of New York, one of the country's most powerful districts for federal prosecutions, opened a grand jury probe into Singham’s finances in June. He has yet to be charged with any crime. HOW CODEPINK CO-FOUNDER MEDEA BENJAMIN'S FAMILY FOUNDATION BECAME A MAJOR FUNDER OF LEFT-WING ACTIVIST GROUPS Trauma psychologist Dr. Orli Peter, who founded the Israel Healing Initiative, a nonprofit that has been providing high-tech trauma treatment for people impacted by the Oct. 7 attack, told Fox News Digital that the demonstrations across the country "manipulate the public," weaponize the anniversary, and detract from the mourning of Jewish people. "Demonstrating while Jews are mourning on Oct. 7 weaponizes the anniversary," Peter explained. "It serves two purposes for the activists: One is to manipulate the public by interrupting the mourning before empathy settles on Jewish suffering and responsibility points to Hamas." articles.title: Trump wants to make his West Palm Beach golf club a permanent presidential retreat
articles.summary: The proposed deal would also make Trump’s club the “permanent United States Presidential Golf Course,” which could be used “by all past, current and future” presidents, the club’s attorney said in a letter.
articles.body: President Donald Trump wants to add a presidential retreat to his club in West Palm Beach, Florida, with his golf course there becoming the “permanent United States Presidential Golf Course.” An attorney for the Trump International Golf Club proposed the designation and construction of a retreat on Trump’s dime in a letter to the Palm Beach County Board of County Commissioners, which has been obtained by NBC News. “Just as Camp David, Windsor Palace or the Elysee Palace are known worldwide, so too will the Presidential Golf Course in Palm Beach County,” Harvey Oyer wrote in the letter last month, which was first reported by The Palm Beach Post. The White House confirmed the proposal to The Washington Post on Wednesday. Trump, asked about the report in the Oval Office, told reporters that it had not been his idea but that he was on board. “This was suggested to me by the military and Secret Service,” and it is “a great idea,” he said. “They asked if I’d be willing to do it, and I said I would be,” he said. “This wouldn’t be for me. This would be for all future presidents,” and it is “one of the best golf courses in the world,” Trump said. Oyer’s letter asks the county, which owns the property the course is on, to give some of the land to the federal government for the project. The club would work with the government to design an “appropriate Presidential lodging facility” that the club would pay to construct. A White House official said in a statement that the retreat could be used for presidents to “hold important meetings and utilize the amenities of a world-class property.” “The property is minutes away from the Donald J. Trump International Airport, does not have buildings looming, does not have houses along the course, has great security features, is close to law enforcement, and happens to be a highly-rated golf course,” the statement said. “These are features that are necessary for any Presidential retreat.” Trump, a frequent golfer who used to mock his predecessor Barack Obama during the 2016 presidential campaign for hitting the links, said Wednesday that “it seems all presidents play golf” and that the new retreat would be “used a lot.” Oyer’s letter said the facility could be used by “all past, current and future U.S. presidents regardless of party affiliation and all visiting heads of state, regardless of party affiliation.” A reporter for Fox News asked Trump whether the retreat would be called “Camp Donald.” “It’s already called Trump International,” he replied.

articles.title: DHS proposes massive $70K fee for foreign students seeking work authorization
articles.summary: DHS proposes a $70,000 OPT fee for F-1 visa holders in the United States, calling the program a pipeline for cheap foreign labor into the workforce.
articles.body: A proposed rule from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) would implement new fees for international students seeking temporary employment in their field of study, an effort the agency says is aimed at reducing the flow of cheap labor into the U.S. Under the proposal, F-1 visa holders would be charged a $70,000 fee for an initial optional practical training (OPT) authorization, as well as a $30,000 fee for any subsequent extension. "Optional practical training was never meant to be a back door into the American workforce, a subsidy for cheap labor or a prize for those who game the system," a DHS spokesperson said. "DHS is upskilling OPT to require foreign students to justify their worth to employers. American workers should not have to compete against a program that has been turned into a pipeline for cheap foreign labor." EXCLUSIVE: ‘PHANTOM EMPLOYEES' SCANDAL SPURS GOP CRACKDOWN ON $36B INCENTIVE FOR COMPANIES TO BYPASS AMERICANS OPT allows eligible foreign students to work part time while enrolled in school and full time for a set period after graduation at a cost of around $500. To participate, students must work in a field directly related to their majors, receive a recommendation from a designated school official (DSO) and obtain employment authorization from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS). TRUMP ADMIN’S FRAUD CRACKDOWN TARGETS FOREIGNERS ACCUSED OF INFILTRATING US FEDERAL PROGRAMS Graduates with degrees in science, technology, engineering or mathematics (STEM) fields can qualify for an additional 24-month extension. DHS said the proposed fee structure comes in response to widespread fraud and abuse identified by the Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP). According to the agency, certain schools, DSOs, employers and F-1 students have exploited existing regulations through illicit arrangements, including non-compliant worksites and "pay-to-stay" visa schemes. The agency maintains that the rule change would force educational institutions to exercise "greater oversight and selectivity" before recommending students for the program. However, the proposal is expected to face immediate legal hurdles. OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE TORPEDOES TRUMP’S BID TO PROTECT US JOBS BY REFORMING CONTROVERSIAL IMMIGRATION POLICY "Don't Panic: DHS has no authority to slap a $70k fee on international students," Doug Rand, director of the Talent Mobility Fund, an organization advocating to attract foreign STEM talent, wrote on LinkedIn. "Let's not overreact — this proposed rule isn't going to fare well in the courts, just as the $100k H-1B fee and other restrictionist policies have been struck down." articles.title: Governador e senador eleitos pelo PL tiveram menos de 100 mil votos de diferença no RS | G1
articles.standfirst: Zucco fez 3.516.048 votos, e Sanderson, 3.453.316 votos, segundo dados da Justiça Eleitoral. A diferença foi de 62,7 mil votos.
articles.summary: Zucco fez 3.516.048 votos, e Sanderson, 3.453.316 votos, segundo dados da Justiça Eleitoral. A diferença foi de 62,7 mil votos.
articles.body:
Luciano Zucco (PL) e Sanderson (PL), governador e senador eleitos para 2027 no RS — Foto: Bruno Todeschini/Agência RBS

O PL foi vitorioso das eleições do Rio Grande do Sul. Elegeu um governador em primeiro turno pela primeira vez desde 2010 no estado, com Luciano Zucco , e elegeu o senador mais votado, com Ubiratan Sanderson .

O futuro governador fez 3.516.048 votos enquanto o senador eleito computou 3.453.316 votos, uma diferença de 62.732 votos.

O PL fez, ainda, a maior bancada da Assembleia Legislativa no RS, com 12 cadeiras, e teve a deputada estadual mais votada: Adri Cherini . Fez o maior número de cadeiras (8) na bancada gaúcha na Câmara e teve o deputado federal mais votado: Maurício Marcon .

O eleitor gaúcho do PL foi fiel ao voto no 22: Zucco e Sanderson tiveram apenas 62,7 mil votos de diferença nas eleições para governador e para o Senado, respectivamente. Eleito em 1º turno com 58,05% dos votos válidos, Zucco teve apenas 1.81% a mais de votos do que Sanderson.

"Adotamos uma estratégia de fixar as duas candidaturas ao Senado à do Zucco ao governo e deu certo. Como temos os mesmos ideais políticos e uma relação de amizade muito grande, não foi difícil do eleitor identificar as 3 candidaturas como uma só", analisa Sanderson.

O atual deputado federal também teve uma votação muito similar ao seu colega de bancada na gaúcha na Câmara dos Deputados e companheiro de chapa, Marcel van Hattem (Novo).

Ambos foram eleitos com pouco mais de 4 mil votos de diferença e Van Hattem conquistou a segunda vaga do Senado com a preferência de 3.449.053 eleitores.

Sanderon recebeu 30,11% dos votos válidos, enquanto Van Hattem teve uma fatia de 30,08% do eleitorado.

articles.title: Critical House race that could decide control of Congress hits home stretch as GOP rep warns what's at stake
articles.summary: Mariannette Miller-Meeks accuses Christina Bohannan of aligning with the Democratic Socialists of America on open borders and defunding police.
articles.body: PRAIRIE CITY, Iowa — Iowa's 1st Congressional District is shaping up to be one of the closest races in the country as Republicans try to hold their razor-thin majority in the House. Fox News Digital spoke to Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks about her pitch to keep the seat in GOP hands and what Democrats taking back control would mean. "Common sense over crazy. This is just common sense over crazy communism," Miller-Meeks told Fox News Digital about her opponent, former Democratic state Rep. Christina Bohannan, who Miller-Meeks said is "perfectly in alignment" with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). Miller-Meeks accused Bohannan, who the National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC) has labeled a "DEI queen," of supporting progressive priorities during her time in the Iowa House that aren't in line with where the majority of Iowa voters stand. HOUSE GOP BILL MOVES TO CLOSE WHISTLEBLOWER GAPS EXPOSED BY MINNESOTA MEDICAID FRAUD SCANDAL "My opponent has not supported law enforcement. She tries to hide where she is on open borders. She has voted against every single tax cut while she was an Iowa legislator and said that the working family's tax cut was dangerous and would get rid of all of it," Miller-Meeks said. "Then she talks about in her campaign ads supporting tax cuts for the middle class. She also supported keeping boys in girls sports and boys and girls locker rooms." Miller-Meeks, who spoke to Fox News Digital at a Department of Agriculture roundtable talking to farmers about their needs and the Trump administration's efforts to lower burdensome farming regulations, said, over the next month until the election, her campaign will continue to "make sure that we're serving Iowans, that were out meeting with constituents answering their questions, coming before them and being available and doing the great constituent work that we've always done and showing the contrast." The incumbent congressman touted her record of working to bring in a massive steel mill in recent months, creating manufacturing jobs, helping farmers through ethanol and biodiesel policies, improving water quality and supporting conservation. DEM IN KEY SWING RACE MISSED NEARLY HALF HER STATE HOUSE VOTES WHILE TAKING TAXPAYER SALARY: 'NO SHOW' Voters across the country, including in Iowa, have expressed frustration with the economy, the cost of gas and diesel and the Iran War. And while Miller-Meeks acknowledged the concerns, she's making the case that putting Democrats back in power isn't the answer because they would roll back the work that has been done by Republicans. "There'll be no relief coming," she said. "They already said that they would get rid of all those policies." Miller-Meeks said the Democratic Party as a whole has moved further left and will attempt to "get rid of" Republican-led measures she credited with making U.S. steel production more competitive and benefiting states like Iowa. "Our bill on opening up energy production here in the United States did bring gasoline prices and diesel prices down at the first of the year," Miller-Meeks explained. She added that if Republican policies had been put in place during the Biden administration, "we would have already had more biodiesel, which would have helped bring down diesel prices." The congresswoman argued Republicans will fight to preserve policies that lower energy, housing, healthcare and prescription drug costs, create jobs and root out fraud, waste and abuse that cost taxpayers millions. "It's not just making prices affordable, but it's also increasing wages and increasing jobs and good-paying jobs," she said. "We have certainly done that with the policies that we've put in place that the Democrats would get rid of." WATCH: BATTLEGROUND DEMOCRAT CALLED IOWA A 'BACKWATER' OVER TRANSGENDER ATHLETES BAN Miller-Meeks also mentioned several proposals she led targeting fraud in government programs following the Feeding Our Future scandal, which raised many questions about accountability among state leaders. The Medicaid Whistleblower Protection Act would establish federal protections nationwide for Medicaid workers who report early warning signs of fraud, and the WALZ Act would require the Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General to open investigations into any program that sees a 10% or greater increase in total payments over any six-month period within a fiscal year. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Tackling corruption inside the government, inside government agencies or in members of Congress or the administration, we're gonna continue to do that and work to serve Iowans and the American people," she said. This will be Bohannan’s third time running for Congress against Miller-Meeks after narrowly losing by less than a percentage point in 2024. The race is rated a "toss up" by Cook Political Report, reflecting Democratic momentum and broader headwinds facing Republicans in a midterm election shaped by President Donald Trump’s approval ratings and economic concerns. In a statement to Fox News Digital, Bohannan defended her positions, writing Miller-Meeks' "siding with drug companies, data centers, billionaires and party leadership at every turn" is "self-serving." "What's crazy is pretending to represent your constituents when you're bought and sold. I'll always put Iowa first. That's common sense," Bohannan said.

articles.title: GOP Senate hopeful sounds alarm after alleged Mall of America terror plot thwarted
articles.summary: Michele Tafoya says Minnesotans "feel under a level of threat" after the FBI arrested an 18-year-old over an alleged ISIS-inspired Mall of America plot.
articles.body: Republican Senate nominee Michele Tafoya says people in her home state of Minnesota "feel under a level of threat" after the FBI arrested an 18-year-old who allegedly pledged allegiance to ISIS and discussed carrying out a mass shooting at the Mall of America. Tafoya, who is aiming to flip a Democrat-controlled open Senate seat as she faces off against Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan in the midterm elections, praised authorities in an X post, writing, "Thank you to @FBIMinneapolis and law enforcement for stopping a potential mass-casualty attack." But she also pointed to the midterms as she argued, "This November, the choice is clear: law and order or more of the same. Common sense or chaos." Authorities said Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud had been under investigation for nearly two years before he was arrested on the spot after buying an AK-47-style rifle, magazines and ammunition from an undercover FBI employee. FBI: MALL OF AMERICA TERROR PLOT THWARTED "This was a radicalized young man who needed to be watched," U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen said Wednesday at a news conference. Rosen added that agents "were able to detect a threat and disrupt it before the defendant carried out his intention to kill, in his words, maybe 30 to 60 people." Mohamud, according to an FBI agent's sworn complaint, repeatedly affirmed in chat messages to the informant that he intended to attack and kill non-Muslims at the mall on Oct. 24, the date of a scheduled Hmong arts celebration. The Hmong are an ethnic group from East and Southeast Asia with a large community in Minnesota." Tafoya, in a Fox News Digital interview, said, "I hear a lot of concerns from Minnesotans on the campaign trail about crime, and no matter what form that crime takes, Minnesotans know that they feel under a level of threat that has increased lately here in Minnesota. "And in the last week and just today, we saw the arrest of an 18-year-old ... American citizen to Somali parents arrested for ... planning a terrorist attack at the Mall of America," Tafoya said, as she referred not only to the thwarting of the terror plot, but also a recent spate of gang gun violence tied to what some in local law enforcement say are members of "the Somali American community." DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB "He basically stated that he wanted to take out anyone who was not a Muslim. He also noted that the Mall of America is owned by people who are Jewish," Tafoya added. "Again, he is of Somalian descent, and terror is alive and well. And thank God we averted this massive crisis." Flanagan, in a statement on X, wrote, "I’m relieved that a horrific attack on Minnesota was prevented and grateful for the actions of law enforcement." Fox News Digital reached out to Flanagan's campaign for more reaction to the terror plot arrest and to Tafoya's comments but didn't receive a response at the time this article was published. Sen. Amy Klobuchar, the Democratic gubernatorial nominee, wrote in a statement, "I'm grateful for the heroic work of law enforcement that prevented a mass shooting and terrorist attack at the Mall of America. This shows why we continue to need major coordinated investments in anti-terrorism and local law enforcement to stop attacks like these." MIDTERM MATH: THE THREE FORCES THAT COULD STOP A DEMOCRATIC BLUE WAVE Klobuchar, who is running to succeed retiring Democratic Gov. Tim Walz, emphasized, "Our state must take terrorism and violent crime head on, working with our federal law enforcement and local police departments to keep Minnesotans safe." "I’m grateful for the work of federal and local law enforcement that stopped this potentially catastrophic ISIS-inspired terrorist plot. It’s frightening to know that a young person could be led down this path," Demuth wrote on X. "It’s fortunate that we have law enforcement officials and members of the U.S. Attorney’s Office that were able to do the work necessary to prevent a terrible act of mass violence from taking place in our community."

articles.title: Trump to award National Medal of Science to Elon Musk
articles.summary: President Trump will award the National Medal of Science to Elon Musk and other prominent tech executives Thursday, a White House official confirmed to The Hill’s broadcast partner, NewsNation. Musk, the head of SpaceX and Tesla, will receive this high honor at the White House’s “Science: A New Golden Age” summit. Three other tech leaders…
articles.body:
President Trump will award the National Medal of Science to Elon Musk and other prominent tech executives Thursday, a White House official confirmed to The Hill’s broadcast partner, NewsNation.

Musk, the head of SpaceX and Tesla , will receive this high honor at the White House’s “Science: A New Golden Age” summit. Three other tech leaders will be presented this award, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su.

The president will also award two people with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation, the nation’s highest honor for technological achievement. Michael Dell, the founder and CEO of Dell Technologies, and Satya Nadella, the CEO of Microsoft, are both set to receive this recognition Thursday.

Fox News was the first to report on these awards.

“The Trump Administration is grateful for the contributions of these incredible leaders in science and technology,” assistant White House press secretary Liz Huston said in a statement. “These recipients are helping ensure America keeps leading the world in innovation.”

All of the honorees have contributed in some way to Trump’s or the Republican Party’s campaigns or causes.

Musk, who briefly joined the Trump administration to lead an effort to reduce the federal workforce, was the president’s largest individual donor for his 2024 campaign. Brin donated large sums to the Republican National Committee in 2025 and appeared at Trump’s second inauguration ceremony.

At the launch of the White House’s “ Trump Accounts ” in July, the president told reporters to “ go out and buy a Dell computer ” after the company’s leader and his wife pledged to donate $6.25 billion to the program. Nvidia also promised to match the Treasury Department’s $1,000 deposits for its employees.

Huang has appeared at high-profile events alongside Trump, including the president’s recent state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Musk was also present at this event.

Musk and Huang were also among the tech leaders who recently signed a White House pledge to self-police the development of advanced artificial intelligence models, amid rising concerns about the dangers this technology could pose to humanity.

articles.body:
President Trump doubled down on his comments suggesting Iran could hit Los Angeles and San Diego during a rally in Texas on Wednesday, adding that the U.S. would not let such a scenario play out.

“You want to see trauma? You want to see problems? And I said it the other day, let them hit a missile into San Diego or Los Angeles on the way. You want to see a horror show? Let them hit San Diego. Let them hit Los Angeles,” Trump said, speaking at a campaign rally in San Antonio.

“You want to see some bad things happen? You want see a country in free fall? We’re not going to let that happen,” he continued.

California leaders lashed out at Trump after he suggested at a rally in Nebraska on Monday that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego.

The state’s Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) told The Hill on Tuesday that Trump was “mentally ill” and called for the 25th Amendment to be invoked.

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass (D) called the comments “dangerous and could potentially compromise our safety,” while San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria (D) said in a statement the city was “not collateral damage.”

However, the White House pushed back fiercely against the characterization of the comments.

“The media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality,” White House communications director Steven Cheung wrote Tuesday on the social platform X.

“He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped. America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money,” he said.

articles.title: Democrats sue US President Trump over taxpayer-funded ad campaign
articles.summary: Trump has faced a bipartisan backlash over ads that critics say violate prohibitions on taxpayer-funded propaganda.
articles.body:
The Democratic National Committee has filed a lawsuit against United States President Donald Trump over television advertisements that were publicly funded and allegedly used to promote his political policies.

Ken Martin, who heads the Democratic Party’s leadership body, suggested in a statement on Wednesday that the ads were designed to bolster Republican odds in the upcoming November 3 midterm elections .

“Donald Trump is misusing millions of taxpayer dollars to fund pure propaganda ads in a last-ditch attempt to save Republicans in November,” Martin said.

Later that day, Common Cause, a democracy watchdog group, filed a second lawsuit over the same set of ads.

It argued that the ads were “overtly political” and therefore ran afoul of laws that bar public funds from being used for political propaganda.

“These ads are not public-service announcements,” Common Cause said in its lawsuit, citing a justification Trump has offered for the television spots. “They are personal publicity and political propaganda through and through.”

Both lawsuits argue that, to create the ad campaign, Trump directed the White House to repurpose $20m in funds that Congress allocated for commemorative activities related to border security, including for those killed in the line of duty.

That manoeuvre, they argue, violates the separation of powers established in the US Constitution.

“The founders made clear more than 200 years ago that the executive can spend money only according to Congress’s direction,” Common Cause’s lawsuit said.

The two lawsuits also point to a provision Congress includes in its appropriations bills barring the use of taxpayer funds for “publicity or propaganda purposes”.

Both complaints seek to have the ads declared illegal, and the expenditures stopped. They also call for steps to be taken to recover any money already spent on the ads.

The Democrats’ lawsuit was filed in Washington, DC, while the Common Cause complaint will be heard in the Southern District of New York.

Trump has faced mounting criticism over the ads, which began airing in September.

So far, the advertising campaign has cost more than $12m to run, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact.

The $20m Trump tapped for the ads comes from a $175m package Congress assigned to the Department of Homeland Security as part of Trump’s immigration enforcement agenda.

Critics have pointed out that one of the ads appears nearly identical to a television spot Trump used in his 2024 re-election campaign.

Three ads have aired so far. In one, a choir sings “love me” over a montage of Trump as he declares the US will “never be a communist country”. Another uses images of Mount Rushmore as Trump heralds a new “golden age of America”.

The third is darker: Trump walks towards the camera in black and white, warning of a “final battle” against the “deep state” and other perceived enemies.

On Wednesday, the news agency Reuters and the research firm Ipsos released a poll showing the ads are highly unpopular . Some 86 percent of the Americans surveyed, including four out of five Republicans, said it was inappropriate for Trump to have used public money for them.

Trump has defended the ads as “promotion for the country”, and he has argued they were similar to public outreach campaigns put out by previous administrations.

But after a bipartisan backlash, Trump said on Monday that taxpayer funds would no longer be used for future ads .

He did not, however, commit to paying back the money already spent on the existing ads.

Members of Trump’s Republican Party have been among those speaking out against the ad campaign.

Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, said the advertisements resembled something former Hungarian leader Viktor Orban would put out.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, meanwhile, indicated he agreed with the message in one of the advertisements, but he emphasised that “it shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars”.

articles.title: Trump says ‘we protect our cities’ after saying Iran could ‘take out’ Los Angeles or San Diego
articles.summary: The president recast his earlier incendiary statements at a San Antonio rally meant to galvanize voters behind Texas Republicans ahead of the midterms.
articles.body: After having faced fierce backlash, President Donald Trump on Wednesday sought to clean up incendiary comments he made earlier this week, when he said Iran could “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego. Trump’s original remarks, made at a campaign rally in Nebraska, seemed to refer to what would happen if Iran had a nuclear weapon. “They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego,” Trump said Monday to cheers from the crowd. He recast those remarks Wednesday night at a rally in San Antonio as he tried to explain the Iran war, saying he had “no choice” if the U.S. were to keep Iran from developing a nuclear weapon. “You want to see problems? And I said it the other day: Let them hit a missile into San Diego or Los Angeles on the way. Let them hit. You want to see a horror show? You want to see problems?” “Let them hit San Diego. Let them hit Los Angeles if you want to see some bad things happen. You want to see a country that would be in free fall?” This time, however, he added: “We’re not going to let that happen. We protect our cities. We protect our country. We’re not letting that happen.” Trump’s initial remarks sparked backlash, particularly from California Democrats. Gov. Gavin Newsom accused Trump of prodding foreign enemies to take out U.S. cities. “He is deranged and dangerous,” Newsom wrote on social media. “To do that makes us look ridiculous on the world stage, but it also gives a green light to Iran, the nation that he chose to attack, the green light to attack our cities,” Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass told NBC News after Wednesday’s rally. Bass said she may call on Congress to investigate Trump’s comments. Trump’s comments Wednesday came in a winding speech at a boisterous rally that stretched for about an hour and 45 minutes, with numerous interruptions from protesters. At one point, a protester who had been heckling Trump was grabbed by a person in the audience in an incident captured on video. A man in the crowd, wearing what looked to be a red “Make America Great Again” hat, grabbed the protester by the hair. Others in the crowd tried to free the protester. The evening was meant to boost Texas Republicans, including Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is running for the Senate in a pitched battle against Democrat James Talarico. In a reflection of Trump’s low favorability ratings, even in the red state of Texas, Gov. Greg Abbott — a staunch Trump ally — said he could not attend because of a scheduling conflict. Capping the night, Trump announced that he would award former Major League Baseball pitcher and seven-time Cy Young Award winner Rogers Clemens the Presidential Medal of Freedom. “We’re giving him the Presidential Medal of Freedom, and along with the Congressional Medal of Honor, it’s the highest award bestowed upon anyone,” Trump said, adding he would help him get into the Baseball Hall of Fame someday. “He deserves it.” Clemens, a Texan, was accused of using performance-enhancing drugs late in his baseball career. He maintains he has never used PEDs. On Wednesday night, Clemens took the stage at Trump’s invitation, saying he was “stunned.” “This supersedes anything that obviously I’ve done in my playing career,” Clemens said. “To get it from this man, this president, there wouldn’t be another president I’d want to get it from.”

articles.title: Trump dominates the Iowa Senate debate from afar
articles.summary: Republican Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek sparred about how to handle the president and other issues in a battleground debate Wednesday night.
articles.body: President Donald Trump was the main character in a televised Iowa Senate debate Wednesday night between Democrat Josh Turek, a state representative, and Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson. Turek hammered Hinson for supporting Trump policies that he says are the culprit in rising costs for Iowa families — from “chaotic tariffs” to the war in Iran — whether they live in cities or on farms. “The real issue is that Iowans are hurting, and they’re hurting uniquely,” Turek said. “I’m hearing ‘I’m struggling to keep food on the table, I’m struggling to pay my electric bill, I’m struggling to keep a roof above my head,’ and now with this war in Iran, ‘I’m struggling just to keep gas in my tank.’” He noted that Hinson voted seven times against curtailing the war and five times against reining in Trump’s tariffs. Hinson fired back, accusing Turek of skipping out on votes in the Legislature, being “too liberal” for the state and lying when he accused her of using her position to enrich her family. “It’s one thing to vote like an East Coast liberal; it’s another to lie like them,” she said. At another point, she jabbed Turek for flip-flopping on his willingness to legislate with Trump. “You trashed the president during the primary, and now you’re doing ads saying you’re going to work with him,” she said. “It’s a tale of two Tureks.” But by modern standards, the debate over a Senate seat that is one of a handful that will determine party control of the chamber was unusually civil. Hinson expressed her sympathy over Turek’s sister’s being diagnosed with cancer, and Turek nodded to the pain negative ads caused both candidates. And both of them pledged to work with Trump or a future Democratic president. “You work with the person who’s going to sign the bills, no matter who that person is, on things that are important to your state, and that’s exactly what I’ve done,” Hinson said. In particular, she pointed to laws President Joe Biden signed on preventing stillbirths and providing mental health services to rural veterans for which she was the lead Republican sponsor in the House. Recent polls have found the race is more or less a dead heat, with several surveys showing each candidate with a lead within the margin of error. Iowa has been a reliably Republican state in recent years, with Trump having won it in all three of his bids for the presidency and the GOP controlling both Senate seats and all four U.S. House seats. But Trump’s low approval ratings have been an anchor on Republican candidates in Iowa, as they have been across the country. Trump was about 1,000 miles south Wednesday night, campaigning in Texas as Hinson and Turek debated in Iowa, but he looms over virtually every contest approaching in the midterm election. The last time Democrats won statewide federal races in Iowa was more than a decade ago, when Barack Obama carried the state in two presidential elections and when then-Sen. Tom Harkin was re-elected to a fifth term in 2008. The Senate seat is open because Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa, is honoring a self-imposed promise to serve only two terms. The one-on-one between Hinson and Turek, part of the Iowa Press debates series, was held at the local PBS studio in Johnston, about 10 miles north of Des Moines, and featured three journalists — from Iowa PBS, the Des Moines Register and The Gazette, a newspaper based in Cedar Rapids — asking questions. Hinson and Turek sparred over taxes, Social Security and immigration, among other issues. Hinson cited border crossings during Biden’s term as a reason Iowans should not trust Turek and Democrats on the issue, arguing that her rival supports “all the illegals.” Trump and Republicans, she said, deserve credit for clamping down on illegal immigration. “We have now sealed off the border, that just took about six months to get that done, and now we have zero crossings happening at our southern border,” she said. “So, who do you trust to fix the problem — the arsonists, the people who started the fire or the people who are cleaning up the mess?” Turek affirmed that he would not vote to fund the Department of Homeland Security without significant changes to immigration enforcement policies, including requiring the use of body cameras and revising use-of-force standards. “Yeah, that is my position,” he said. He added that he believes that no one wants to see “Americans shot in the street,” a reference to federal officers’ killing Renee Good and Alex Pretti during an immigration crackdown in Minnesota this year. “What I am talking about is we can have safe and secure borders, and we need to have a pathway to earn citizenship for those that have come here legally,” Turek said. At several points, Turek accused Hinson of slashing Medicaid, Obamacare premium subsidies and food assistance funds to cut taxes for the wealthiest Americans. Hinson responded that she was proud to eliminate taxes on tips, overtime pay and Social Security checks, which were among the features of Trump’s signature “big, beautiful bill” last year. Turek said he supports those provisions, but he also proposed eliminating the cap on Social Security taxes to keep the program solvent beyond the six-year time frame when benefits are expected to be reduced if Congress does not act. That cap currently shields income above $184,500 per year from Social Security taxes. “I think that it is fundamentally wrong that you have every single teacher and police officer and firefighter that is paying payroll tax and Social Security tax year-round,” Turek said. “Meanwhile, you’ve got folks like Elon Musk and Bill Gates and Jeff Bezos that are paying just for the first few minutes of the year. The best way we can keep this solvent is by taking off the cap.” Hinson countered that lifting the cap would not fully fund Social Security payouts and argued that a federal commission should be established to revamp the system and keep it solvent. Congress, which holds the actual authority to rewrite the Social Security law, would then vote on the commission’s plan. “This is a serious issue for our seniors, and it is a promise we need to keep to them,” she said, accusing Turek of “fearmongering” on the issue. The candidates ducked and weaved a little on the last questions posed to them. Hinson was asked whether Congress is abdicating its authority by allowing Trump to build a White House ballroom and promise to send $5,000 payments to Americans if Republicans win the House and the Senate. “Well, speaking as someone who serves on the Appropriations Committee right now, I care very deeply about Article I of the Constitution, which is making sure that we have the power of the purse,” she said, without addressing whether Trump’s seizure of that authority is proper. Turek declined to rule out voting to remove Trump from office if he is impeached by the House. “I have no interest in looking at impeachment,” he said in response to a question. “I think that we need to look forward, not back.” In a twist at a time when many Democratic Senate candidates are distancing themselves rhetorically from Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., Hinson said she could team up with him if Democrats win the majority and she wins the Iowa Senate seat. “So, hopefully it’s not Chuck Schumer, but if it’s Chuck Schumer, I’ll work with him,” she said. “I got things across the line with [Rep.] Nancy Pelosi [D-Calif.] as speaker, so I think that shows that I can work with anyone.” Earlier in the debate, she sought to undermine Turek’s boast that he is not taking money from corporate PACs by highlighting the Schumer-backed super PACs that have taken money from companies and spent heavily to help elect Turek. “He is basically taking laundered corporate PAC money,” she said, challenging Turek to call for ads on his behalf to be taken down “if you don’t want to take that corporate PAC money, because that’s how it flows. It flows through people like Chuck Schumer, right to support you.” Turek declined to denounce the political action committees backing him.

articles.title: Turek, Hinson spar in first Iowa Senate debate: 3 takeaways
articles.summary: U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) and state Rep. Josh Turek (D-Iowa), the two candidates for Senate, faced off in a debate Wednesday night, where health care cuts and agriculture were significant topics, as well as each candidate’s voting record and attendance in their current roles. Hinson and Turek are running to replace retiring Sen. Joni…
articles.body:
U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) and state Rep. Josh Turek (D-Iowa), the two candidates for Senate, faced off in a debate Wednesday night, where health care cuts and agriculture were significant topics, as well as each candidate’s voting record and attendance in their current roles.

Hinson and Turek are running to replace retiring Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa). Hinson, 43, was a broadcast journalist before running for office in 2017. Turek, 47, is a professional wheelchair basketball player and state legislator.

The race is one of the most competitive in the country, as evidenced by tight polling , “toss-up” ratings by nonpartisan analysts and fundraising. The debate comes one night after the Hawkeye State’s gubernatorial candidates, Rob Sand (D) and Zach Lahn (R), sparred in their own contentious debate .

It’s the sixth-most expensive Senate contest in terms of advertising, with $90 million spent so far in total on ads. This was the first debate between them before the general election.

Both candidates want to end the Iran war, citing fuel prices

The war in Iran is a critical issue for battleground races across the country this year, but is playing a significant role in agricultural heartland states like Iowa. Turek called out Hinson for her early support of the war and President Trump’s tariffs, both of which Democrats say are responsible for high everyday costs nationwide.

“We’re looking at diesel prices being at an all-time high as our farmers are going into harvesting time and leading to a furthering increase of input costs, like fertilizer,” Turek said, adding Iowa farmers are telling him it affects their bottom lines and that “I certainly don’t want to see Iran have a nuclear weapon, but we have to end this war.”

Turek also compared the Iran war to the war in Vietnam, mentioning his father’s exposure to the chemical weapon Agent Orange, which caused Turek to be born with spina bifida, a physical disability that requires him to use a wheelchair.

Hinson recently called for the Iran war to end, citing its effect on high prices in Iowa. In the debate, she mentioned her teenage sons, saying she wanted a quick end to prevent the further loss of American troops.

“I don’t want this to be a forever war, so I want to make sure we do everything we can,” Hinson said. “I trust in our U.S. military, the greatest fighting force in the world, to bring this to a close as quickly as possible, because I know people are getting squeezed.”

When asked why she voted against resolutions to end the war, Hinson said it would have created too quick of a withdrawal that could have endangered troops.

“I don’t think we need another resolution, and I certainly don’t want to see the president not be able to do an orderly end to this war,” Hinson said. “You look at what happened when President Biden did the withdrawal hastily out of Afghanistan, and we lost 13 service members, including an Iowan, at Abbey Gate.”

Both leaned into bipartisan records and times they broke from their own party

Turek said he does not support Congress pursuing another impeachment of Trump when asked, but that instead lawmakers should focus on passing legislation to lower costs.

“I have no interest in looking at impeachment,” Turek said. “I think that we need to look forward, not back.”

Turek is running as a moderate Democrat and emphasizing his record of voting with Republicans in the statehouse. During the debate, he mentioned areas of agreement with Trump, like the prohibitions of taxes on tips, overtime and Social Security and the need for a “safe and secure” southern border.

“I’m the only one up on this stage that has actually worked across the aisle to address immigration,” said Turek, referring to his 2024 vote to criminalize some immigration violations.

“If you have come here illegally and you have committed violent crimes, you should no longer be here,” Turek added, while also mentioning he did not support the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement tactics.

“At the same time, I think we can recognize that we need to have a pathway to earn citizenship for those that have come here legally, and I do think that we, you know, I think we can all agree that we don’t want to see Americans shot in the street.”

Hinson, for her part, has generally backed Trump’s immigration enforcement moves. But she emphasized legislation she worked on with Democrats, such as bills on maternal healthcare and veterans’ mental health that President Biden signed into law.

“I’ll be President Trump’s ally when it is important for Iowa, but I will push back on him, he knows this because I talk to him regularly, on things that are wrong for our state,” Hinson said. “That’s true no matter who is governing and who has the gavel. So hopefully it’s not Chuck Schumer, but if it’s Chuck Schumer, I’ll work with him. I got things across the line with Nancy Pelosi as Speaker, so I think that shows that I can work with anyone.”

Both attacked on missed or controversial votes and campaign finance

Both Turek and Hinson have voting records that the other has used for easy attack. Turek has missed many votes in the state legislature, more than most other members, and that’s something Hinson has been eager to point out in her ads .

But Hinson, as a congresswoman, has voted for some controversial legislation, like the “One, Big, Beautiful Bill,” or H.R. 1, which included Medicaid cuts estimated to cause more than 11 million people nationwide to be uninsured by 2034. She has also voted against measures that would have directed Trump to remove troops from Iran.

Hinson doubled down on Turek’s missed votes, while Turek tied the health care cuts to Iowa’s growing cancer crisis.

“He was one of the most absent, and he was one of the most liberal when he did show up to vote,” Hinson said of Turek, briefly mentioning immigration and Turek’s opposition to a measure that would set a higher bar for raising taxes.

“She voted for 110,000 Iowans to lose their healthcare in a state with a cancer crisis and a healthcare crisis,” Turek said in response to a later question. “I think that that is fundamentally wrong.”

Both candidates also brought up campaign finance and specifically, corporate donors, an issue that has come up in other races around the country. Turek attacked Hinson over her increased personal wealth while in office, which Hinson said is related to her husband’s sale of his insurance business in 2021.

“More liberal lies from liberal allies, allies of Josh Turek,” Hinson said. “We decided to sell our individual stocks right away in 2021, so we made it very clear that I want Iowans to know the decisions that I’m making in Washington D.C. have nothing to do with the inside information I might be getting as a public servant.”

She added that she supports a stock trading ban for members of Congress, which Turek also backs. He noted that he does not currently own any stocks.

“The reality is, is that in just six years of being up in D.C., Ashley Hinson is up to 15 times more wealthy, still owns up to $5 million of private stock, even though she said she was going to sell everything,” Turek said. “This is the corruption that we have to address.”
